n: In a fallen world, things that cause people to stumble will happen. But Jesus warns that those who lead others into sin carry a heavy responsibility.

f.g: Greek skandala — stumbling blocks, traps that cause someone to fall into sin.

n: It would be better to be drowned with a heavy stone tied around one’s neck than to cause a vulnerable or new believer to fall away.

f.g: A large stone used for grinding grain.
Children, and also humble or new disciples.

n: Watch yourselves. If someone wrongs you, address it honestly; if they repent, forgive them. Correction and forgiveness work together.

f.g: Sin against, wrong.

n: Even if it happens seven times in one day, keep forgiving. There is no limit on forgiveness for the repentant.
Hearing how high the standard is, the apostles plead: give us more faith!

Jesus replies that even tiny faith — like a mustard seed — can do the impossible, like commanding a deep-rooted tree to replant itself in the sea. The issue is not the size of faith but its genuineness.

f.g: A black mulberry tree, known for its deep, extensive roots.

f.w: faith as a grain of mustard seed

n: Jesus describes a servant coming in from plowing or shepherding. Would his master tell him to sit down and eat first?

f.g: Immediately (the older English meaning).

n: No — the master would expect him to prepare dinner and serve first, then eat afterward.

f.g: Eat supper.
Tuck in your robe and get ready to serve.

n: The master doesn’t thank the servant for simply doing what was expected.

f.g: I think not.

n: Likewise, when we obey God, we haven’t earned special credit — we’ve done our duty. Service done in humility, not pride, pleases God. King Benjamin taught the same.
Still traveling toward Jerusalem, Jesus passes along the border region between Samaria and Galilee.

f.w: the midst of Samaria and Galilee
f.g: Probably along the boundary between the two regions.

n: Ten men with leprosy meet Him at a village, keeping their distance as the law required of those with skin diseases.

f.g: People with a contagious skin disease (not always modern leprosy) who were isolated from society.

n: They shout together for mercy. Shared suffering has erased the line between Jew and Samaritan.

f.g: Greek epistatēs, “chief” or “commander.”

n: Jesus tells them to go show themselves to the priests — the procedure for someone already healed. As they obey in faith, they are cleansed on the way.
One of them, realizing he is healed, turns back, loudly praising God.

f.g: The same word used for repentance — turning around.

n: He falls at Jesus’ feet in gratitude. Luke saves a twist for the end: this grateful man is a Samaritan, an outsider.
Jesus asks: weren’t ten healed? Where are the other nine?
Only this foreigner came back to give glory to God. Gratitude is rarer than blessings.

f.g: Foreigner — one not of Israel.

n: Jesus tells him to rise and go: his faith has made him whole. All ten were cleansed in body, but this one received something more — wholeness and salvation.

f.g: Greek sōzō — saved, healed, made complete.

n: The Pharisees ask when God’s kingdom will arrive. Jesus says it won’t come with dramatic signs to be watched for and charted.

f.g: With visible signs that can be watched for and calculated.

n: No one will need to point “here” or “there,” because the kingdom is already among them — present in Jesus Himself.

f.g: Greek can mean “in your midst.” JST Luke 17:21: “the kingdom of God has already come unto you.”

n: Jesus warns His disciples of coming days when they will long for even one day of His presence and will not have it.

f.w: the days of the Son of man
f.g: The time of Jesus’ presence — now in mortality and later at His coming.

n: People will claim the Messiah is here or there. Don’t chase after them. False Christs will come.
His Second Coming won’t be a secret: it will be as unmistakable as lightning flashing across the whole sky.
But before glory comes suffering. He must first suffer greatly and be rejected by His own generation.

f.w: first must he suffer many things

n: The world at His coming will be like the world in Noah’s day.

f.g: Greek form of the name Noah.

f.w: as it was in the days of Noe

n: People carried on with normal life — eating, drinking, marrying — paying no attention to warnings until the flood swept them away.

f.w: until the day that Noe entered into the ark

n: Lot’s day was the same: buying, selling, farming, and building, unaware of what was coming.

f.g: Built.

n: The very day Lot left Sodom, fire and sulfur rained down and destroyed the city.

f.g: Sulfur, which burns with intense heat.

n: It will be just like that when the Son of Man is revealed — sudden, while people are absorbed in ordinary life.

f.g: Unveiled, made fully visible.

f.w: the day when the Son of man is revealed

n: On that day, don’t go back for possessions. Someone on the roof shouldn’t go down for belongings; someone in a field shouldn’t turn back.

f.g: Belongings.

n: Just three words: Remember Lot’s wife. She looked back with longing at what she left and was lost.
Clinging to this life means losing it; giving it up for God means keeping it.

f.g: Literally “keep it alive.”

n: On that night, two people may share a bed; one will be taken and one left. Judgment will divide even the closest companions.
Two women grinding grain together — one taken, the other left. Life will be going on as usual.

f.g: Women commonly ground grain together at a hand mill each morning.

n: Two men working in a field — one taken, one left. Readiness is personal; no one can be prepared for another.

f.w: Two men shall be in the field
f.g: This verse is absent from many early Greek manuscripts but appears in Matthew 24:40.

n: The disciples ask where this will happen. Jesus answers with a proverb: where the carcass is, the vultures gather. The JST explains that the “body” is where the Saints are gathered.

f.g: Greek aetos can mean eagles or vultures.
